claim: Proper brain development relies highly on protein N-glycosylation to sustain neuronal migration, axon guidance and synaptic physiology.
source: Proper brain development relies highly on protein N-glycosylation to sustain neuronal migration, axon guidance and synaptic physiology.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of N-glycosylation in brain development, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Impairing the N-glycosylation pathway at early steps produces broad neurological symptoms identified in congenital disorders of glycosylation.
source: Impairing the N-glycosylation pathway at early steps produces broad neurological symptoms identified in congenital disorders of glycosylation.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG) and their clinical manifestations.

claim: Srd5a3 deletion causes mild N-glycosylation impairment without significantly altering ER homeostasis.
source: Srd5a3 deletion causes mild N-glycosylation impairment without significantly altering ER homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study, including lectin blotting and transcriptomic analysis showing no significant ER stress response.

claim: Srd5a3 loss affects a subset of glycoproteins with high N-glycans multiplicity per protein and decreased protein abundance or N-glycosylation level.
source: Srd5a3 loss affects a subset of glycoproteins with high N-glycans multiplicity per protein and decreased protein abundance or N-glycosylation level.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic and glycoproteomic data showing enrichment of highly glycosylated proteins among those with decreased abundance.

claim: IgSF-CAM adhesion proteins are critical for neuron adhesion and highly N-glycosylated.
source: As IgSF-CAM adhesion proteins are critical for neuron adhesion and highly N-glycosylated, we observed impaired IgSF-CAM-mediated neurite outgrowth and axon guidance in Srd5a3 mutant cerebellum.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about IgSF-CAM proteins and their roles in neural development.

claim: Impaired IgSF-CAM-mediated neurite outgrowth and axon guidance occurs in Srd5a3 mutant cerebellum.
source: As IgSF-CAM adhesion proteins are critical for neuron adhesion and highly N-glycosylated, we observed impaired IgSF-CAM-mediated neurite outgrowth and axon guidance in Srd5a3 mutant cerebellum.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from granule cell culture experiments and electron microscopy showing aberrant parallel fiber orientation.

claim: High N-glycan multiplicity is linked to fine-tuned neural cell adhesion during mammalian brain development.
source: Our results link high N-glycan multiplicity to fine-tuned neural cell adhesion during mammalian brain development.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data showing that highly glycosylated proteins, particularly IgSF-CAMs, are preferentially affected in the mutant.

claim: Nearly all proteins transported through the secretory pathway undergo N-glycosylation.
source: Nearly all proteins transported through the secretory pathway undergo N-glycosylation, particularly to regulate cell surface abundance and cellular interactions(Dennis et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dennis et al., 2009.

claim: N-glycosylation particularly regulates cell surface abundance and cellular interactions.
source: Nearly all proteins transported through the secretory pathway undergo N-glycosylation, particularly to regulate cell surface abundance and cellular interactions(Dennis et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dennis et al., 2009.

claim: Protein N-glycosylation is a template-independent process that shows distinct glycosylation patterns varying by protein and physiological context.
source: This template-independent process shows distinct glycosylation patterns that vary by protein and physiological context(Dennis et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dennis et al., 2009.

claim: Protein N-glycosylation begins in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) where a lipid-linked oligosaccharide (LLO) precursor is synthesized.
source: Protein N-glycosylation begins in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), where a tightly controlled and conserved biosynthetic pathway synthesizes a precursor named the lipid-linked oligosaccharide (LLO).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the N-glycosylation pathway.

claim: The LLO comprises a sequential assembly of 14 monosaccharides (Glc3Man9GlcNAc2) on top of the phosphorylated lipid carrier dolichol.
source: This LLO comprises a sequential assembly of 14 monosaccharides (Glc3Man9GlcNAc2) on top of the phosphorylated lipid carrier dolichol.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structure of the LLO precursor.

claim: The oligosaccharyltransferase (OST) complex transfers en bloc the oligosaccharide part of the LLO to Asn residues on specific sites (Asn-X-Ser/Thr, X≠Pro) in nascent glycoproteins.
source: Then, the oligosaccharyltransferase (OST) complex transfers en bloc the oligosaccharide part of the LLO to Asn residues on specific sites (Asn-X-Ser/Thr, X≠Pro) in nascent glycoproteins(Chavan and Lennarz, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chavan and Lennarz, 2006.

claim: N-linked glycan undergoes final modifications in the ER and Golgi compartments.
source: N-linked glycan undergoes final modifications in the ER and Golgi compartments.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the N-glycosylation pathway.

claim: Disrupting the N-glycosylation process in humans causes congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG).
source: Disrupting the N-glycosylation process in humans causes congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG), a wide and highly heterogeneous group of inherited metabolic disorders (Ng and Freeze, 2018) (Freeze et al., 2014) (Jaeken and Péanne, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to Ng and Freeze, 2018; Freeze et al., 2014; and Jaeken and Péanne, 2017.

claim: CDG is a wide and highly heterogeneous group of inherited metabolic disorders.
source: Disrupting the N-glycosylation process in humans causes congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG), a wide and highly heterogeneous group of inherited metabolic disorders (Ng and Freeze, 2018) (Freeze et al., 2014) (Jaeken and Péanne, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to Ng and Freeze, 2018; Freeze et al., 2014; and Jaeken and Péanne, 2017.

claim: Disrupted synthesis or transfer of LLO underlies the most prevalent disorder, CDG type I (CDG-I).
source: Among them, disrupted synthesis or transfer of LLO underlies the most prevalent disorder, CDG type I (CDG-I)(Jaeken and Péanne, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jaeken and Péanne, 2017.

claim: CDG-I diagnosis is based on the detection of hypoglycosylation of the patients' serum transferrin that exhibits unoccupied N-glycosylation site(s).
source: CDG-I diagnosis is based on the detection of hypoglycosylation of the patients' serum transferrin that exhibits unoccupied N-glycosylation site(s).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CDG-I diagnosis.

claim: CDG-I disorders present psychomotor retardation as the most common feature.
source: Clinically, CDG-I disorders present psychomotor retardation (the most common feature) associated with cerebellar ataxia, seizures, retinopathy, liver fibrosis, coagulopathies, abnormal fat distribution and failure to thrive.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the clinical presentation of CDG-I.

claim: CDG-I disorders are associated with cerebellar ataxia, seizures, retinopathy, liver fibrosis, coagulopathies, abnormal fat distribution and failure to thrive.
source: Clinically, CDG-I disorders present psychomotor retardation (the most common feature) associated with cerebellar ataxia, seizures, retinopathy, liver fibrosis, coagulopathies, abnormal fat distribution and failure to thrive.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the clinical presentation of CDG-I.

claim: Cerebellar ataxia is the primary diagnostic indicator in patients with PMM2 mutations (PMM2-CDG, also known as CDG-Ia disorder).
source: Cerebellar ataxia is the primary diagnostic indicator in patients with PMM2 mutations (PMM2-CDG, also known as CDG-Ia disorder), which is the most frequent CDG (Schiff et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schiff et al., 2017.

claim: PMM2-CDG is the most frequent CDG.
source: Cerebellar ataxia is the primary diagnostic indicator in patients with PMM2 mutations (PMM2-CDG, also known as CDG-Ia disorder), which is the most frequent CDG (Schiff et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schiff et al., 2017.

claim: Phenotypic defects in CDG may arise from unoccupied glycosylation sites (i.e. protein hypoglycosylation) in numerous and mostly unidentified proteins.
source: These phenotypic defects may arise from unoccupied glycosylation sites (i.e. protein hypoglycosylation) in numerous and mostly unidentified proteins.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from the known biochemical defect in CDG.

claim: The efficacy of protein glycosylation relies on the primary sequence at the glycosylation site (i.e. the sequon), the neighboring amino acids and the local structure.
source: The efficacy of protein glycosylation relies on the primary sequence at the glycosylation site (i.e. the sequon), the neighboring amino acids and the local structure (Poljak et al., 2018) (Murray et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Poljak et al., 2018 and Murray et al., 2015.

claim: In CDG, the limited amount of LLO can impact glycosylation site occupancy to cause hypoglycosylation.
source: In CDG, the limited amount of LLO, the OST complex substrate, can also impact glycosylation site occupancy to cause hypoglycosylation (Burda and Aebi, 1999) (Freeze et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Burda and Aebi, 1999 and Freeze et al., 2015b.

claim: Initial studies investigated the consequences of metabolic defects in CDG mainly in serum.
source: Initial studies investigated the consequences of this metabolic defect mainly in serum (Hülsmeier et al., 2007) (Richard et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hülsmeier et al., 2007 and Richard et al., 2009.

claim: Tissue accessibility and technical limitations precluded examining defects in organs, specifically the developing brain.
source: However, tissue accessibility and technical limitations precluded examining defects in organs, specifically the developing brain (Freeze et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Freeze et al., 2015b.

claim: N-glycans have well-known importance in specific phases of neural development.
source: The lack of data related to the consequence of the defect at the proteomic level contrasts with the well-known importance of N-glycans in specific phases of neural development (Scott and Panin, 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Scott and Panin, 2014b.

claim: Several CDG models showing neural developmental defects exist, but the mis-glycosylated targets remain unidentified.
source: While several CDG models showing neural developmental defects exist, the mis-glycosylated targets remain unidentified (Chan et al., 2016; Cline et al., 2012; Scott and Panin, 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chan et al., 2016; Cline et al., 2012; and Scott and Panin, 2014a.

claim: Some glycoproteins possess a proclivity for hypoglycosylation based on their intrinsic properties.
source: We predict that some glycoproteins possess a proclivity for hypoglycosylation based on their intrinsic properties (Poljak et al., 2018) (Hülsmeier et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a prediction based on citations to Poljak et al., 2018 and Hülsmeier et al., 2007.

claim: SRD5A3 is an enzyme involved in LLO synthesis and is mutated in CDG type I patients (SRD5A3-CDG).
source: Previous studies identified SRD5A3, an enzyme involved in LLO synthesis, as mutated in CDG type I patients (SRD5A3-CDG) (Cantagrel et al., 2010) (Morava et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cantagrel et al., 2010 and Morava et al., 2010.

claim: SRD5A3 is a steroid-reductase-like enzyme involved in the last step of de novo synthesis of dolichol.
source: SRD5A3 is a steroid-reductase-like enzyme involved in the last step of de novo synthesis of dolichol, the lipid used to build the LLO precursor.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SRD5A3 function.

claim: The broad clinical spectrum observed in patients with SRD5A3 mutations shows many similarities with other ER-related glycosylation defects including psychomotor retardation and cerebellar ataxia.
source: The broad clinical spectrum observed in patients with SRD5A3 mutations shows many similarities with other ER-related glycosylation defects including psychomotor retardation and cerebellar ataxia.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about SRD5A3-CDG clinical presentation.

claim: Symptoms in SRD5A3-CDG result from likely null SRD5A3 alleles.
source: These symptoms result from likely null SRD5A3 alleles (Kara et al., 2014; Tuysuz et al., 2016) (Wheeler et al., 2016) (Cantagrel et al., 2010) (Gründahl et al., 2012) and reflect impaired protein N-glycosylation, as previously described in yeast and mouse embryos mutated for the corresponding SRD5A3 ortholog (Cantagrel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to Kara et al., 2014; Tuysuz et al., 2016; Wheeler et al., 2016; Cantagrel et al., 2010; and Gründahl et al., 2012.

claim: Symptoms in SRD5A3-CDG reflect impaired protein N-glycosylation, as previously described in yeast and mouse embryos mutated for the corresponding SRD5A3 ortholog.
source: These symptoms result from likely null SRD5A3 alleles (Kara et al., 2014; Tuysuz et al., 2016) (Wheeler et al., 2016) (Cantagrel et al., 2010) (Gründahl et al., 2012) and reflect impaired protein N-glycosylation, as previously described in yeast and mouse embryos mutated for the corresponding SRD5A3 ortholog (Cantagrel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cantagrel et al., 2010.

claim: Homozygous germline mutants (Srd5a3-/-) are embryonic lethal.
source: Homozygous germline mutants (Srd5a3-/-) are embryonic lethal (data not shown) consistent with results from the Srd5a3 gene-trap mutant (Cantagrel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study and a citation to Cantagrel et al., 2010.

claim: En1-Cre; Srd5a3fl/- mice were fertile and showed nearly Mendelian ratios at weaning age.
source: En1-Cre; Srd5a3fl/- mice were fertile and showed nearly Mendelian ratios at weaning age (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Total protein extracts from mutant cerebellums showed a non-significant 12% decrease in normalized SNA signal intensity.
source: Total protein extracts from mutant cerebellums showed a non-significant 12% decrease in normalized signal intensity (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Similar results were obtained with Concanavalin A (ConA) lectin that binds to core and immature mannosylated N-glycans.
source: We obtained similar results with Concanavalin A (ConA) lectin that binds to core and immature mannosylated N-glycans (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: Cerebellar Srd5a3 deletion does not cause a severe general glycosylation defect.
source: These results indicate that cerebellar Srd5a3 deletion does not cause a severe general glycosylation defect.
evidence: This is inferred from the lectin blotting data showing only mild changes in glycosylation.

claim: Lamp1 indicated a severe decrease in protein levels across different tissues in Srd5a3 mutants.
source: However, Lamp1, a broadly used marker for N-glycosylation defects (Rujano et al., 2017) (Kretzer et al., 2016), indicated a severe decrease in protein levels across different tissues (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C–E and citations to Rujano et al., 2017 and Kretzer et al., 2016.

claim: The remaining Lamp1 showed a shift toward a lower molecular weight before PNGase treatment, which indicated impaired glycosylation.
source: The remaining Lamp1 showed a shift toward a lower molecular weight before PNGase treatment, which indicated impaired glycosylation (Figure 1D,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D,F.

claim: En1-Cre; Srd5a3fl/- mice showed a severe and highly significant (p=0.0007) motor coordination defect assessed with the rotarod test.
source: In contrast, En1-Cre; Srd5a3fl/- mice showed a severe and highly significant (p=0.0007) motor coordination defect assessed with the rotarod test (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: En1-Cre; Srd5a3fl/- mice showed a mild impairment of working memory in the Morris Water Maze test.
source: The latency to reach the platform was significantly lower on the second trial than on the first one for control mice, but not for En1-Cre; Srd5a3fl/- mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I). This result suggests a mild impairment of working memory in the mutant mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: A significant hypoplasia was observed in the En1-Cre; Srd5a3fl/- mice cerebellum.
source: We observed a significant hypoplasia in the En1-Cre; Srd5a3fl/- mice (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A–D.

claim: Examining the mutant cerebellum cytoarchitecture revealed an accumulation of scattered ectopic cell clusters in the external part of the molecular layer (ML).
source: Examining the mutant cerebellum cytoarchitecture revealed an accumulation of scattered ectopic cell clusters in the external part of the molecular layer (ML; Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The ectopic clusters were NeuN-positive, post-mitotic granule cells (GCs) that failed to migrate to the internal granule cell layer (IGL).
source: These clusters were NeuN-positive, post-mitotic granule cells (GCs) (Figure 2F) that failed to migrate to the internal granule cell layer (IGL).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Atoh1-Cre; Srd5a3fl/- mice exhibit similar GC ectopias although in a lesser extent compared to the En1-Cre; Srd5a3fl/- mice.
source: Atoh1-Cre; Srd5a3fl/- mice exhibit similar GC ectopias although in a lesser extent compared to the En1-Cre; Srd5a3fl/- mice (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: The GC ectopia observation indicates a partial GC-autonomous defect.
source: This observation indicates a partial GC-autonomous defect and could be explained by the involvement of GC glycoproteins and non-GC interactors that interplay to allow GCs to initiate their migration and prevent the formation of these ectopic clusters.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of En1-Cre and Atoh1-Cre mutant phenotypes.

claim: Total proteomic analysis quantified 1982 proteins in P7 mouse cerebellum.
source: This approach quantified 1982 proteins, whose abundance profiles can cluster each sample by genotype (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Statistical analysis identified 97 differentially abundant proteins (DAP) (≈ 5% of the total; q-value <0,05) in the En1-Cre; Srd5a3fl/- mice.
source: Our statistical analysis identified 97 differentially abundant proteins (DAP) (≈ 5% of the total; q-value <0,05) in the En1-Cre; Srd5a3fl/- mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Over-representation analysis indicated that different pathways involved in ion and amino acid transport, synapse function, cell adhesion-related signaling and cholesterol biosynthesis interplay to generate the mouse phenotype.
source: Our analysis indicated that different pathways involved in ion and amino acid transport, synapse function, cell adhesion-related signaling and cholesterol biosynthesis interplay to generate the mouse phenotype (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by over-representation analysis of the DAP shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Aside from changes in cholesterol metabolism, all enriched pathways contained at least one deregulated N-glycoprotein.
source: Aside from changes in cholesterol metabolism, all enriched pathways contained at least one deregulated N-glycoprotein.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the DAP and their classification as N-glycoproteins.

claim: No enrichment in the ER stress pathway was found among the 97 DAP.
source: Protein N-glycosylation is critical for ER-protein folding, however we did not find any enrichment in the ER stress pathway.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the DAP for ER stress-related proteins.

claim: Manual inspection of the 97 DAP revealed increased levels of only two ER-stress-related proteins, SDF2L1 and HYOU1.
source: Manual inspection of the 97 DAP revealed increased levels of only two ER-stress-related proteins, SDF2L1 (Fujimori et al., 2017) and HYOU1 (Zhao et al., 2010), while BiP, the classical ER-stress marker(Ron and Walter, 2007), showed a 1.3 fold non-significant (q = 0.08) increase (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Supplementary file 1 and citations to Fujimori et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2010; and Ron and Walter, 2007.

claim: BiP showed a 1.3 fold non-significant (q = 0.08) increase in the mutant cerebellum.
source: Manual inspection of the 97 DAP revealed increased levels of only two ER-stress-related proteins, SDF2L1 (Fujimori et al., 2017) and HYOU1 (Zhao et al., 2010), while BiP, the classical ER-stress marker(Ron and Walter, 2007), showed a 1.3 fold non-significant (q = 0.08) increase (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Supplementary file 1 and a citation to Ron and Walter, 2007.

claim: Transcriptomic study confirmed the absence of any significant deregulation of the most widely used UPR markers.
source: We then performed a transcriptomic study on additional samples at the same stage, which confirmed the absence of any significant deregulation of the most widely used UPR markers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: No change in BIP levels was observed restricted to ectopic GC clusters.
source: In addition, we did not observe any change in BIP levels restricted to ectopic GC clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: The results exclude a main effect of deregulated N-glycosylation processes on ER stress.
source: Surprisingly, our results exclude a main effect of deregulated N-glycosylation processes on ER stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of ER stress markers in the proteomic and transcriptomic data.

claim: A significant, 4-fold enrichment of N-glycoproteins was observed among the DAP with decreased levels (p=0.0012).
source: We observed a significant, 4-fold enrichment of N-glycoproteins among the DAP with decreased levels (simplified as decreased N-glycoproteins; p=0.0012, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Decreased N-glycoproteins have more N-glycosylation sites (i.e. higher site multiplicity) with an average of 5.57 sites versus 3.24 in unchanged N-glycoproteins.
source: Examining this group of decreased N-glycoproteins revealed that they have more N-glycosylation sites (i.e. higher site multiplicity) with an average of 5.57 sites versus 3.24 in unchanged N-glycoproteins (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: N-glycoproteins with four or more N-glycosylation sites are significantly enriched within the decreased N-glycoproteins.
source: Indeed, N-glycoproteins with four or more N-glycosylation sites are significantly enriched within the decreased N-glycoproteins (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The mild glycosylation defect detected in the Srd5a3 mutant cerebellum disrupts the levels of highly glycosylated proteins, but does not disrupt ER homeostasis.
source: These data demonstrate that the mild glycosylation defect detected in the Srd5a3 mutant cerebellum disrupts the levels of highly glycosylated proteins, but does not disrupt ER homeostasis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the proteomic and transcriptomic data.

claim: Glycoproteome analysis identified 1404 glycopeptides detected in at least 3 out of 4 control samples.
source: In total, we identified 1404 glycopeptides detected in at least 3 out of 4 control samples (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Samples could be clustered according to the genotype based on the expression levels of all the glycopeptides.
source: As we observed for the total proteome, we could cluster the samples according to the genotype based on the expression levels of all the glycopeptides (see Materials and method, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: For 15% of the N-glycopeptides detected in glycoproteomics (n = 206), decreased levels were found in the mutant samples.
source: For 15% of the N-glycopeptides detected in glycoproteomics (n = 206), we found decreased levels in the mutant samples.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the glycoproteomics analysis.

claim: Of the 206 decreased N-glycopeptides, only 24 were detected in the previous total proteomic experimental settings.
source: Of these, we only detected 24 N-glycopeptides in the previous total proteomic experimental settings, consistent with the high enrichment observed with the glycoproteomics analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Among the 24 N-glycopeptides detected in both analyses, 13 were never detected in control but only in mutant samples in total proteomics.
source: Among these peptides, 13 were never detected in control but only in mutant samples in total proteomics. These data indicate that these 13 peptides were not glycosylated in the mutant.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the comparison of total proteomics and glycoproteomics.

claim: Most differences detected in the glycoproteomic experiment reflect reduced glycosylation site occupancy.
source: We conclude that most differences we detected in the glycoproteomic experiment reflect reduced glycosylation site occupancy.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of total proteomics and glycoproteomics data.

claim: An extremely significant correlation exists between N-glycan multiplicity and N-glycopeptide levels (Mann-Whitney test, p-value<0.0001).
source: We also detected an extremely significant correlation between N-glycan multiplicity and N-glycopeptide levels (Figure 4B, Mann-Whitney test, p-value<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A mild effect of the presence of a non-aromatic amino-acid (other than Phe, Tyr, His or Trp) at position −2 was identified in reduced occupancy sites.
source: We identified a mild effect of the presence of a non-aromatic amino-acid (other than Phe, Tyr, His or Trp) at position −2 and a more significant effect of the Serine at position +2 (Figure 4D), as previously described(Gavel and Heijne, 1990; Murray et al., 2015), with an increased impact in highly glycosylated proteins (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and citations to Gavel and Heijne, 1990 and Murray et al., 2015.

claim: A more significant effect of the Serine at position +2 was identified in reduced occupancy sites.
source: We identified a mild effect of the presence of a non-aromatic amino-acid (other than Phe, Tyr, His or Trp) at position −2 and a more significant effect of the Serine at position +2 (Figure 4D), as previously described(Gavel and Heijne, 1990; Murray et al., 2015), with an increased impact in highly glycosylated proteins (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D,E and citations to Gavel and Heijne, 1990 and Murray et al., 2015.

claim: N-glycan multiplicity combined with sequon efficiency is a major parameter driving protein sensitivity to N-glycosylation defects.
source: These findings demonstrate that N-glycan multiplicity combined with sequon efficiency is a major parameter driving protein sensitivity to N-glycosylation defects.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the glycoproteomics data showing effects of both multiplicity and sequon characteristics.

claim: Over-representation analysis revealed that the most significantly affected proteins (4 out of the top 10 deregulated pathways) derive directly from cell adhesion and axon guidance-related pathways involving adhesion proteins from the L1CAM family.
source: This analysis revealed that the most significantly affected proteins (4 out of the top 10 deregulated pathways) derive directly from cell adhesion and axon guidance-related pathways involving adhesion proteins from the L1CAM family (Figure 5A, red circles).
evidence: This is supported by over-representation analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: L1CAMs and the previously identified NCAM1 and CNTN2 belong to the immunoglobulin superfamily of cell adhesion molecules (IgSF-CAMs) with critical roles in brain development.
source: L1CAMs and the previously identified NCAM1 and CNTN2 (Figure 3B) belong to the immunoglobulin superfamily of cell adhesion molecules (IgSF-CAMs) with critical roles in brain development (Maness and Schachner, 2007; Pollerberg et al., 2013; Stoeckli, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Maness and Schachner, 2007; Pollerberg et al., 2013; and Stoeckli, 2010.

claim: The particular sensitivity of IgSF-CAMs to a N-glycosylation defect arises from their higher N-glycosylation site multiplicity with an average of 3.3 sites versus 2.3 in non IgSF-CAM proteins.
source: We speculate that this particular sensitivity of IgSF-CAMs to a N-glycosylation defect arises from their higher N-glycosylation site multiplicity with an average of 3.3 sites versus 2.3 in non IgSF-CAM proteins (Calculated based on the reference glycoproteomic dataset, Supplementary file 2, Mann Whitney test, p-value<0.0001).
evidence: This is a speculation based on analysis of the reference glycoproteomic dataset.

claim: There is enrichment for IgSF-CAMs glycopeptides within the decreased ones (Fisher exact test, p-value=0.0058).
source: We confirmed the enrichment for IgSF-CAMs found in our over-representation analysis at the N-glycopeptide level (18.4% of the decreased N-glycopeptides belong to an IgSF-CAM protein, Fisher exact test, p-value=0.0058, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A clear hypoglycosylation defect for L1CAM and NrCAM was observed with a detected shift to lower molecular weights.
source: We did observe a clear hypoglycosylation defect for L1CAM and NrCAM with a detected shift to lower molecular weights and a significant decrease in the glycosylation-dependent cleavage of L1CAM (Lutz et al., 2014) (Figure 5C,D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C,D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and a citation to Lutz et al., 2014.

claim: A significant decrease in the glycosylation-dependent cleavage of L1CAM was observed.
source: We did observe a clear hypoglycosylation defect for L1CAM and NrCAM with a detected shift to lower molecular weights and a significant decrease in the glycosylation-dependent cleavage of L1CAM (Lutz et al., 2014) (Figure 5C,D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C,D and a citation to Lutz et al., 2014.

claim: A major role for IgSF-CAMs in mammalian development is illustrated by the increased number of their encoding genes across evolution.
source: A major role for IgSF-CAMs in mammalian development is illustrated by the increased number of their encoding genes across evolution (Hortsch, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hortsch, 2000.

claim: An increase in the N-glycan multiplicity for three IgSF-CAM families with critical roles in brain development was observed across evolution.
source: We also observed an increased in the N-glycan multiplicity for three IgSF-CAM families with critical roles in brain development (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The multiplicity of IgSF-CAM glycoproteins is almost systematically much higher in mammals compared to the other species.
source: The multiplicity of these glycoproteins is almost systematically much higher in mammals compared to the other species.
evidence: This is based on analysis of multiplicity data across species shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Human L1CAM and NrCAM immuno-blotting profiles exhibit clear shifts in SRD5A3-/- CPNs.
source: As previously observed in mouse, human L1CAM and NrCAM immuno-blotting profiles exhibit clear shifts in SRD5A3-/- CPNs (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The sensitivity of highly glycosylated IgSF-CAMs to SRD5A3 loss is conserved across mammalian species.
source: These data demonstrated a similar exacerbated sensitivity of IgSF-CAMs to SRD5A3 loss in human neurons. Our data suggest that the sensitivity of highly glycosylated IgSF-CAMs to N-glycosylation defect is conserved across mammalian species and that the increase in multiplicity during evolution parallels the acquisition of a more complex neural cell organization.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of mouse and human data.

claim: The increase in multiplicity during evolution parallels the acquisition of a more complex neural cell organization.
source: Our data suggest that the sensitivity of highly glycosylated IgSF-CAMs to N-glycosylation defect is conserved across mammalian species and that the increase in multiplicity during evolution parallels the acquisition of a more complex neural cell organization.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed correlation between multiplicity and evolutionary complexity.

claim: A 30.8% decrease in L1CAM cell surface expression was detected in Srd5a3 cKO neurons.
source: We detected the expression of these IgSF-CAMs along the axons and at the growth cone but with 30.8% and 39.6% decrease for L1CAM and NrCAM, respectively, in Srd5a3 cKO neurons (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: A 39.6% decrease in NrCAM cell surface expression was detected in Srd5a3 cKO neurons.
source: We detected the expression of these IgSF-CAMs along the axons and at the growth cone but with 30.8% and 39.6% decrease for L1CAM and NrCAM, respectively, in Srd5a3 cKO neurons (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: A similar defect in cell surface expression was recapitulated using Tunicamycin.
source: We recapitulated a similar defect using Tunicamycin suggesting that the disruption of other steps of the N-glycosylation pathway as well as specific drugs can efficiently alter the cell-surface expression of these glycoproteins.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from tunicamycin treatment experiments.

claim: A 38.5% decrease in the binding of L1CAM chimera was observed in mutant cells.
source: Indeed, a 38.5% and 56.0% decrease in the binding of L1CAM and NrCAM chimeras, respectively, was observed in mutant cells (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: A 56.0% decrease in the binding of NrCAM chimera was observed in mutant cells.
source: Indeed, a 38.5% and 56.0% decrease in the binding of L1CAM and NrCAM chimeras, respectively, was observed in mutant cells (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: The glycosylation level of IgSF-CAMs plays a critical role in the regulation of their cell-surface expression.
source: This result validates the functional impact of IgSF-CAMs hypoglycosylation and suggests that the glycosylation level of IgSF-CAMs plays a critical role in the regulation of their cell-surface expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing decreased cell surface expression and binding in mutant cells.

claim: NrCAM and L1CAM show redundant functions in cerebellar GC development, in addition to their roles in axonal growth.
source: Among proteins identified in our proteomic approaches, NrCAM and L1CAM show redundant functions in cerebellar GC development, in addition to their roles in axonal growth (Sakurai et al., 2001) (Demyanenko et al., 1999) (Demyanenko et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sakurai et al., 2001; Demyanenko et al., 1999; and Demyanenko et al., 2011.

claim: CNTN2/TAG-1 contributes to neuronal polarization and axonal organization.
source: CNTN2/TAG-1 contributes to neuronal polarization and axonal organization.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CNTN2 function.

claim: The corresponding CNTN2 KO mouse shows ectopic GC clusters at the pial surface of the cerebellum.
source: Interestingly, the corresponding KO mouse shows ectopic GC clusters at the pial surface of the cerebellum (Xenaki et al., 2011), as observed in the Srd5a3 mutant cerebellum.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Xenaki et al., 2011.

claim: Mice lacking Cntn1 show aberrant parallel fibers distribution and motor coordination defects.
source: Mice lacking Cntn1 show aberrant parallel fibers distribution and motor coordination defects (Berglund et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Berglund et al., 1999.

claim: The observed neuronal adhesion defects arise from a cumulative effect of partial hypoglycosylation of multiple interacting partners.
source: Since neural IgSF-CAMs largely bind to each other homophilically and heterophilically (Pollerberg et al., 2013), we suspect that the observed neuronal adhesion defects arise from a cumulative effect of partial hypoglycosylation of multiple interacting partners (Schwarz et al., 2009) (Stoeckli et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a speculation based on citations to Pollerberg et al., 2013; Schwarz et al., 2009; and Stoeckli et al., 1997.

claim: IgSF-CAMs show increased complexity and members in vertebrates.
source: IgSF-CAMs show increased complexity and members in vertebrates (Vogel and Chothia, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vogel and Chothia, 2006.

claim: The increased diversity in some IgSF-CAM proteins correlates with the presence of homologs with higher multiplicity in mammals.
source: The increased diversity in some IgSF-CAM proteins correlates with the presence of homologs with higher multiplicity in mammals (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A positive selection of adhesion proteins with high N-glycosylation site multiplicity can support the increased complexity of mammalian neuronal organization and connectivity.
source: We speculate that a positive selection of adhesion proteins with high N-glycosylation site multiplicity can support the increased complexity of mammalian neuronal organization and connectivity.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed correlation between multiplicity and evolutionary complexity.

claim: Highly glycosylated IgSF-CAM members play critical roles in the developing eyes and immune system.
source: In addition to the central nervous system, highly glycosylated IgSF-CAM members also play critical roles in other systems affected in CDG patients, such as the developing eyes (Morava et al., 2009) and immune system with ICAM1 (Blank et al., 2006; He et al., 2014), or in other diseases like cancer, where L1CAM plays a critical role in tumor metastasis (Kiefel et al., 2012) (Agrawal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Morava et al., 2009; Blank et al., 2006; He et al., 2014; Kiefel et al., 2012; and Agrawal et al., 2017.

claim: L1CAM plays a critical role in tumor metastasis.
source: In addition to the central nervous system, highly glycosylated IgSF-CAM members also play critical roles in other systems affected in CDG patients, such as the developing eyes (Morava et al., 2009) and immune system with ICAM1 (Blank et al., 2006; He et al., 2014), or in other diseases like cancer, where L1CAM plays a critical role in tumor metastasis (Kiefel et al., 2012) (Agrawal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kiefel et al., 2012 and Agrawal et al., 2017.

claim: Suboptimal functioning of the ER-glycosylation machinery impairs primarily highly glycosylated N-glycoproteins with mild or no effect on ER homeostasis.
source: In conclusion, our study demonstrates that suboptimal functioning of the ER-glycosylation machinery impairs primarily highly glycosylated N-glycoproteins with mild or no effect on ER homeostasis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from the study.

claim: The prevalent neurological symptoms observed in SRD5A3-CDG patients and likely other types of CDG type I result from defective neural cell adhesion, caused by IgSF-CAM hypoglycosylation.
source: We propose that the prevalent neurological symptoms observed in SRD5A3-CDG patients and likely other types of CDG type I result from defective neural cell adhesion, caused by IgSF-CAM hypoglycosylation.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the experimental findings linking IgSF-CAM hypoglycosylation to neuronal defects.

claim: En1-Cre; Srd5a3fl/- GCs showed defective neurite sprouting with a 20% decrease when using a coating with laminin and poly-D-lysine.
source: In contrast, GCs showed defective neurite sprouting with a 20% decrease when using a coating with laminin and poly-D-lysine (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: A 37% reduction in neurite number for mutant GCs compared to control was observed on L1CAM substrate.
source: We observed a 37% and 52% reduction in neurite number for mutant GCs compared to control, on L1CAM and NrCAM substrates, respectively (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: A 52% reduction in neurite number for mutant GCs compared to control was observed on NrCAM substrate.
source: We observed a 37% and 52% reduction in neurite number for mutant GCs compared to control, on L1CAM and NrCAM substrates, respectively (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: When aggregates were plated on L1CAM-coated surfaces, a major defect in both neurite number and subsequent cell migration was observed.
source: However, when the aggregates were plated on L1CAM-coated surfaces, a major defect in both neurite number and subsequent cell migration was observed (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The correct glycosylation of IgSF-CAM is critical for neurite outgrowth, especially in the initiation step.
source: This result highlights the substrate specificity of the adhesion phenotype and overall these data show that the correct glycosylation of IgSF-CAM is critical for neurite outgrowth, especially in the initiation step.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from neurite outgrowth assays.

claim: GCs axons development is a process CNTN2 dependent that precedes the initiation of GCs migration towards the IGL.
source: Interestingly, GCs axons development is a process CNTN2 dependent that precedes the initiation of GCs migration towards the IGL (Xenaki et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Xenaki et al., 2011.

claim: Srd5a3 mutant mice exhibit an aberrant orientation of groups of PFs in the outer ML, likely due to defective axonal guidance.
source: However, Srd5a3 mutant mice exhibit an aberrant orientation of groups of PFs in the outer ML, likely due to defective axonal guidance (Figure 7F,G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F,G.

claim: IgSF-CAMs hypoglycosylation may underlie many neurological defects in CDG.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that IgSF-CAMs hypoglycosylation may underlie many neurological defects in CDG.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: SRD5A3 acts at the last step of dolichol synthesis and facilitates also the synthesis of O-mannose-linked glycans, C-mannosylation, and glycophosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchored proteins.
source: SRD5A3 acts at the last step of dolichol synthesis and facilitates also the synthesis of O-mannose-linked glycans, C-mannosylation, and glycophosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchored proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SRD5A3 function.

claim: N-glycosylation is the most demanding cellular process with eight dolichol molecules needed for each N-linked glycan.
source: However, N-glycosylation is the most demanding cellular process with eight dolichol molecules needed for each N-linked glycan(Cantagrel and Lefeber, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cantagrel and Lefeber, 2011.

claim: Defects in SRD5A3 alter lipid membrane composition that subsequently impairs protein N-glycosylation.
source: Defects in SRD5A3 alter lipid membrane composition that subsequently impairs protein N-glycosylation.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about SRD5A3 function and its role in dolichol synthesis.

claim: Several enzymes from the cholesterol/mevalonate pathway were found deregulated, consistent with previous results using Srd5a3 gene-trapped embryos.
source: Consistently with previous results using Srd5a3 gene-trapped embryos(Cantagrel et al., 2010), several enzymes from the cholesterol/mevalonate pathway were found deregulated (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and a citation to Cantagrel et al., 2010.

claim: A regulatory mechanism could alleviate glycosylation defects by stimulating the mevalonate pathway.
source: These observations indicate a regulatory mechanism that could alleviate these glycosylation defects by stimulating the mevalonate pathway (Haeuptle et al., 2011) (Welti, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculation based on citations to Haeuptle et al., 2011 and Welti, 2013.

claim: Changes in N-glycosylated proteins and correlations between the N-glycan number and peptides abundance strongly implicate the N-glycosylation pathway as the major metabolic target underlying the phenotype and neurological symptoms in SRD5A3-CDG.
source: While we cannot exclude defects in other glycosylation pathways, our results demonstrate that changes in N-glycosylated proteins and correlations between the N-glycan number and peptides abundance in both proteomic and glycoproteomic analyses strongly implicate the N-glycosylation pathway as the major metabolic target underlying the phenotype and neurological symptoms in SRD5A3-CDG.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the proteomic and glycoproteomic data.

claim: A potential mechanism of adaptation to mild glycoprotein folding impairment is detected with the over-expression of the HYOU1 and SDF2L1 chaperones.
source: A potential mechanism of adaptation to this mild impairment is detected with the over-expression of the HYOU1 and SDF2L1 chaperones.
evidence: This is inferred from the proteomic data showing increased levels of these chaperones.

claim: Proteins with high N-glycan multiplicity, estimated to four or more sites, show an increased risk for hypoglycosylation to induce protein degradation or dysfunction.
source: Our work shows that proteins with high N-glycan multiplicity, estimated to four or more sites, show an increased risk for hypoglycosylation to induce protein degradation or dysfunction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the proteomic data showing enrichment of highly glycosylated proteins among those with decreased abundance.

claim: Differences in the sequon can have an additive effect to the increased risk from high multiplicity.
source: Moreover, differences in the sequon can have an additive effect to this increased risk.
evidence: This is based on the glycoproteomic data showing effects of sequon characteristics on site occupancy.

claim: Decreased glycoprotein abundance is a direct consequence of incomplete glycosylation of highly glycosylated proteins.
source: Our total proteomic analysis clearly indicates that decreased glycoprotein abundance is a direct consequence of incomplete glycosylation of highly glycosylated proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the total proteomic data.

claim: Examining L1CAM did not reveal significant differences in full-length isoform abundance by western blot but showed altered cleavage as well as reduced cell surface expression as a consequence of its hypoglycosylation.
source: Yet, examining individual proteins, such as the IgSF-CAM member L1CAM, did not reveal significant differences in full-length isoform abundance by western blot but showed altered cleavage as well as reduced cell surface expression as a consequence of its hypoglycosylation.
evidence: This is based on western blot and immunocytochemistry data.

claim: The cleaved L1CAM isoform (70 kDa) enhances cerebellar GC neurite outgrowth.
source: The cleaved L1CAM isoform (70 kDa) enhances cerebellar GC neurite outgrowth(Lutz et al., 2014), which indicates that hypoglycosylation of some proteins can impair their processing, trafficking and/or functioning without necessarily causing significant changes in their cellular abundance.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lutz et al., 2014.

claim: Hypoglycosylation of some proteins can impair their processing, trafficking and/or functioning without necessarily causing significant changes in their cellular abundance.
source: The cleaved L1CAM isoform (70 kDa) enhances cerebellar GC neurite outgrowth(Lutz et al., 2014), which indicates that hypoglycosylation of some proteins can impair their processing, trafficking and/or functioning without necessarily causing significant changes in their cellular abundance.
evidence: This is inferred from the L1CAM data showing altered cleavage without major changes in total abundance.

claim: The number of N-glycans, in conjunction with their degree of branching, regulates cell proliferation and differentiation.
source: The number of N-glycans, in conjunction with their degree of branching, regulates cell proliferation and differentiation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about N-glycan function.

claim: Highly glycosylated growth factor receptors show increased cell-surface expression by forming galectin-mediated molecular lattices.
source: Highly glycosylated growth factor receptors show increased cell-surface expression by forming galectin-mediated molecular lattices(Lau et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lau et al., 2007.

claim: Neuronal galectin-IgSF-CAM interactions remain unreported.
source: To our knowledge, neuronal galectin-IgSF-CAM interactions remain unreported.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The role for the polysialic acid modification of NCAM1 N-glycan chains is established.
source: However, we still understand very poorly how N-glycans contribute to these functions with few exceptions such as the established role for the polysialic acid modification of NCAM1 N-glycan chains(Weinhold et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Weinhold et al., 2005.

claim: Specific N-glycosylated residues, alpha2,3-linked sialic acid and Lewis(x) of L1CAM, CNTN1 and CNTN2 have been reported to mediate interaction with the glycopeptide CD24 modulating cell adhesion and neurite outgrowth of cerebellar neurons.
source: Interestingly, specific N-glycosylated residues, alpha2,3-linked sialic acid and Lewis(x) of L1CAM, CNTN1 and CNTN2 have been reported to mediate interaction with the glycopeptide CD24 modulating cell adhesion and neurite outgrowth of cerebellar neurons (Lieberoth et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lieberoth et al., 2009.

claim: Highly glycosylated IgSF-CAM members play critical roles in the developing eyes.
source: In addition to the central nervous system, highly glycosylated IgSF-CAM members also play critical roles in other systems affected in CDG patients, such as the developing eyes (Morava et al., 2009) and immune system with ICAM1 (Blank et al., 2006; He et al., 2014), or in other diseases like cancer, where L1CAM plays a critical role in tumor metastasis (Kiefel et al., 2012) (Agrawal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Morava et al., 2009.

claim: ICAM1 plays a critical role in the immune system.
source: In addition to the central nervous system, highly glycosylated IgSF-CAM members also play critical roles in other systems affected in CDG patients, such as the developing eyes (Morava et al., 2009) and immune system with ICAM1 (Blank et al., 2006; He et al., 2014), or in other diseases like cancer, where L1CAM plays a critical role in tumor metastasis (Kiefel et al., 2012) (Agrawal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Blank et al., 2006 and He et al., 2014.

claim: The glycoproteomic enrichment identified 140 likely new glycosylation sites (≈8% of the total).
source: Using this dataset, we identified 140 likely new glycosylation sites (≈8% of the total, see Materials and method, Supplementary file 2) with high recurrence of non-canonical sequons (≈40% of the new sites, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the glycoproteomics analysis.

claim: High recurrence of non-canonical sequons (≈40% of the new sites) was observed among the likely new glycosylation sites.
source: Using this dataset, we identified 140 likely new glycosylation sites (≈8% of the total, see Materials and method, Supplementary file 2) with high recurrence of non-canonical sequons (≈40% of the new sites, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the glycoproteomics analysis.

claim: Most proteins carrying the newly identified glycosylation sites are intrinsic to membrane as observed for proteins with previously identified glycosylation sites.
source: Most proteins carrying these sites are intrinsic to membrane as observed for proteins with previously identified glycosylation sites (Gene Ontology analysis in Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on Gene Ontology analysis of the glycoproteomics data.
